name: Sleep on your back (anti-wrinkle)
lead: Sleeping on the back is promoted in skincare and looksmaxxing circles as a free way to avoid 'sleep lines' and one-sided facial compression. The idea is that a face lying flat is not pressed into a pillow for hours each night, so skin is not folded or pushed in the same place repeatedly.[1][3]

A 2016 literature review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal, led by plastic surgeon Goesel Anson, argued that facial tissue is pushed, pulled and compressed during side or stomach sleeping, that sleep wrinkles differ from expression wrinkles in origin, location and direction, and that avoiding facial distortion, for example by back sleeping, is the reliable way to minimise them.[3] The authors acknowledged that changing sleep habits is difficult and called for more study.[3]

Wikipedia lists habitual sleeping position among factors contributing to skin wrinkles, alongside aging, sun damage and facial expressions.[1] Back sleeping also has health associations, including more positional sleep apnea and reflux in some people.[2] On looksmax.org, members debate whether side sleeping changes facial symmetry or wrinkles and how to learn to sleep supine.[4][5]

chain: Sleep face-up so the face is not pressed into the pillow
Less repeated compression and creasing of facial skin
angle.text: People who adopt back sleeping do so to keep facial skin from being folded against a pillow for hours each night, aiming at fewer sleep creases and a more even look on both sides of the face. Some pair it with a pillow arrangement that keeps the face off the bed.

infobox: Fewer sleep lines and less one-sided compression
Anson et al., Aesthetic Surgery Journal, 2016[3]

paras: The practice involves sleeping supine, sometimes with a pillow arrangement to keep the face off the bed. The Wikipedia article on wrinkles names habitual sleeping position as a contributing factor and points to a dermatology educational page.[1]

Healio's report on the 2016 review says the authors described sleep wrinkles as forming where skin buckles under external pressure, with habitual sleep patterns able to reinforce expression lines, and noted that specialty pillows designed to reduce facial distortion exist.[3]

The 2016 review examined how wrinkles develop from intrinsic and extrinsic influences, concluding that shear, compression and tension forces act on facial tissue during side or stomach sleeping, and that these forces may contribute to facial aging because of the many hours spent asleep.[3] The lead author disclosed a partnership with a company selling a sleep-wrinkle pillow, and the review is a literature analysis rather than a trial.[3]

A looksmax.org thread on side versus back sleeping states that side sleeping contributes at most slightly to asymmetry, that only a few studies suggest it might lead to wrinkles or droopier eyelids over time, and that bone structure is not meaningfully changed by sleeping on one side.[4]
Supine sleeping is linked to more positional obstructive sleep apnea, sleep paralysis and reflux when lying flat after eating, and side sleeping is the most common adult position.[2]
Forum members share ways to sleep supine, including a thread recommending a hammock, which drew replies about spinal support.[5] A Hacker News thread asked how to learn to sleep on the back.[6]

No studies found comparing sleeping positions to wrinkle formation in controlled trials. The 2016 Aesthetic Surgery Journal literature review discusses the mechanical forces on the face during sleep.[3]

timeline.event: Anson and colleagues publish a literature review on sleep-related facial wrinkles in Aesthetic Surgery Journal.[3]

lore.intro: Back sleeping appears in skincare and looksmaxxing discussion as a free anti-aging habit, alongside debate about side sleeping and asymmetry.[4][5]

claims.claim: Side and stomach sleeping cause lasting sleep wrinkles
claims.believers: Proponents say repeated facial compression creases skin over years, a view echoed by the 2016 review's authors.[3]
claims.experts: The 2016 review is a literature analysis, and Wikipedia lists sleeping position among contributing habits citing educational material rather than a trial.[1][3]

claims.believers: Proponents say keeping the face off the pillow avoids creasing, and the 2016 review recommends back sleeping to avoid facial distortion.[3]
claims.experts: No controlled trial testing this was found; supine sleeping has documented apnea and reflux associations.[2]

claims.believers: Forum members say sleeping on one side changes symmetry.[4]
claims.experts: A looksmax.org poster wrote that the effect is slight and that genetics, dental issues and development play a larger role.[4]

card.summary: Sleeping face-up to dodge sleep lines; plausible habit, untested for wrinkles.
card.note: Supine sleep can worsen sleep apnea and reflux in some people.

quick.overview:
The idea is to sleep on your back so the face is not pressed into a pillow. It is claimed to prevent sleep lines.

Sleeping position is listed as a wrinkle factor, but no trial was found.
quick.mechanism: Avoiding pressure and folding of facial skin during sleep.
quick.risks: Supine sleeping is associated with sleep apnea, reflux and sleep paralysis in some people.
